This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of amphibolite and granulite facies base- ment rocks across a 60 km wide north--south traverse through the Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt in West Greenland, which incorporates the c. 2500 Ma Itivdleq shear belt, the c. 1800 Ma Ikert6q shear belt, and adjoining terrains. It also integrates the results with earlier investigations of the belt to produce a composite record of the magnetic field during uplift and cooling of the terrain through c. 600--500°C at c. 1750--1600 Ma. Progressive a.f. and thermal cleaning of samples from 81 sites identifies a range of magnetic components. Lowest blocking temperature remanences in Nagssugtoqidian (c. 1700 Ma) amphibolite facies rocks yield steep W to N positive components residing in magnetite. V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: esults are in general accord with an earlier, less precise, study by one of the authors and indicate a small polar shift between rocks of the Mamainse Point Formation (186 ° E, 38°N) and the Michipicoten Island Formation (175°E, 26°N). A quartz-feldspar porphyry intruding the lower Mamainse Point Formation but unconformably overlain by the Michipicoten Island Formation was sampled for U-Pb zircon dating. The zircons define an age of emplacement of 1086.5 + 1.3/- 3.0 Ma. This age and the pole positions are consistent with, and supplement ages previously determined for the Keweenawan paleomagnetic polar wander curve. These data define an apparent polar wander rate of 14 cm a -1. This age, combined with previously published U-Pb ages, indicates a time span of ~ 22 Ma for most Keweenawan igneous activity. In addition, the time of the Keween- awan paleomagnetic reversal is constrained to be between 1086.5 + 1.3/- 3.0 and 1097.6 +_ 3.6 Ma, the age of the upper part of the reversely magnetized Osier Group. The zircon population contained an inherited component from a source 1403 _ 50 Ma old. This suggests that the porphyry magma was at least partly derived by melting of an anorogenic pluton emplaced during the mid-Proterozoic. The zircon population contained an inherited component from a source 1403 _ 50 Ma old. This suggests that the porphyry magma was at least partly derived by melting of an anorogenic pluton emplaced during the mid-Proterozoic. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. CONCLUSIONS In this paper we have used palaeomagnetic data to facilitate middle and upper Proterozoic stratigraphic correlations and relationships between North 75 China and Yangzi blocks in eastern China. These data appear to be in fair accordance with geological evidence. It should be noted, however, that the data and interpretations are of a preliminary nature and will no doubt change as the data base is expanded and improved. They do suggest, how- ever, that palaeomagnetic and magnetostratigraphic data have great poten- tial for resolving problems in Precambrian stratigraphy and tectonics. teristics provide impor- tant data relating to the sequential history of the Earth's magnetic field and the relative positions of crustal blocks. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. Studies of APW paths, especially "loops", pole positions, palaeolatitudes and reversed polarity zones, taken in conjunction with geochronological palaeontological and geological data (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Ziqiang et al., 1980), suggest that a few magnetostrati- graphic marker beds might be present. Such markers may permit detailed correlations over wide areas. Several such marker beds are shown in the magnetostratigraphic correla- tion scheme (Table II): (1) Yangzhuang--Taizi magnetic marker bed. CONCLUSIONS In this paper we have used palaeomagnetic data to facilitate middle and upper Proterozoic stratigraphic correlations and relationships between North 75 China and Yangzi blocks in eastern China. These data appear to be in fair accordance with geological evidence. It should be noted, however, that the data and interpretations are of a preliminary nature and will no doubt change as the data base is expanded and improved. They do suggest, how- ever, that palaeomagnetic and magnetostratigraphic data have great poten- tial for resolving problems in Precambrian stratigraphy and tectonics. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. teristics provide impor- tant data relating to the sequential history of the Earth's magnetic field and the relative positions of crustal blocks. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. CONCLUSIONS In this paper we have used palaeomagnetic data to facilitate middle and upper Proterozoic stratigraphic correlations and relationships between North 75 China and Yangzi blocks in eastern China. These form the basis for a proposed strati- graphic subdivision of the middle and upper Proterozoic in China. - tematic studies of late Precambrian rocks ranging in age from 1900 Ma to 600 Ma. CONCLUSIONS In this paper we have used palaeomagnetic data to facilitate middle and upper Proterozoic stratigraphic correlations and relationships between North 75 China and Yangzi blocks in eastern China. It should be noted, however, that the data and interpretations are of a preliminary nature and will no doubt change as the data base is expanded and improved. They do suggest, how- ever, that palaeomagnetic and magnetostratigraphic data have great poten- tial for resolving problems in Precambrian stratigraphy and tectonics. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. CONCLUSIONS In this paper we have used palaeomagnetic data to facilitate middle and upper Proterozoic stratigraphic correlations and relationships between North 75 China and Yangzi blocks in eastern China. teristics provide impor- tant data relating to the sequential history of the Earth's magnetic field and the relative positions of crustal blocks. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. Studies of APW paths, especially "loops", pole positions, palaeolatitudes and reversed polarity zones, taken in conjunction with geochronological palaeontological and geological data (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Ziqiang et al., 1980), suggest that a few magnetostrati- graphic marker beds might be present. Tianjin 300170 (People's Republic of China) (Received May 16, 1984; revision accepted July 13, 1984) ABSTRACT Zhang, H. and Zhang, W., 1985. Palaeomagnetic data, late Precambrian magnetostrati- graphy and tectonic evolution of eastern China. Precambrian Res., 29:65--75. In this paper middle and upper Proterozoic (1900--1600 Ma) APW paths are presented for North and South China based on palaeomagnetic results obtained from the Jixian, Yangzi Gorges, Shennongjia and Fuzhou areas in eastern China. Two or three "loops" are present; the second of these has an age of about 1000--800 Ma and is probably roughly equivalent to the Sveconorwegian and Grenville loops. APW paths, loops, reversed polari- ty zones and pole positions, combined with geological data, permit definition of several markers that are useful in regional correlation. These form the basis for a proposed strati- graphic subdivision of the middle and upper Proterozoic in China. A tentative palaeogeo- graphic map has been drawn for the North China and Yangzi Blocks for the period fr

- tematic studies of late Precambrian rocks ranging in age from 1900 Ma to 600 Ma. These studies have been carried out at Jixian, Yangzi Gorges, Shennongjia and in the Fuzhou area where there is good exposure and the structure is relatively simple. These sections are suitable for measurement of remanent magnetization in the rocks. They are also the stratotype and para- stratotype sections for middle and upper Proterozoic rocks in China (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang, Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Zigiang et al., 1980; Chen Jinbiao et al,, 1981). 0301-9268/85/$03.30 © 1985 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. teristics provide impor- tant data relating to the sequential history of the Earth's magnetic field and the relative positions of crustal blocks. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. Studies of APW paths, especially "loops", pole positions, palaeolatitudes and reversed polarity zones, taken in conjunction with geochronological palaeontological and geological data (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Ziqiang et al., 1980), suggest that a few magnetostrati- graphic marker beds might be present. Such markers may permit detailed correlations over wide areas. Several such marker beds are shown in the magnetostratigraphic correla- tion scheme (Table II): (1) Yangzhuang--Taizi magnetic marker bed. In this paper middle and upper Proterozoic (1900--1600 Ma) APW paths are presented for North and South China based on palaeomagnetic results obtained from the Jixian, Yangzi Gorges, Shennongjia and Fuzhou areas in eastern China. Two or three "loops" are present; the second of these has an age of about 1000--800 Ma and is probably roughly equivalent to the Sveconorwegian and Grenville loops. APW paths, loops, reversed polari- ty zones and pole positions, combined with geological data, permit definition of several markers that are useful in regional correlation. These form the basis for a proposed strati- graphic subdivision of the middle and upper Proterozoic in China. A tentative palaeogeo- graphic map has been drawn for the North China and Yangzi Blocks for the period fr

- tematic studies of late Precambrian rocks ranging in age from 1900 Ma to 600 Ma. These studies have been carried out at Jixian, Yangzi Gorges, Shennongjia and in the Fuzhou area where there is good exposure and the structure is relatively simple. These sections are suitable for measurement of remanent magnetization in the rocks. We raise several points to support the theory that the west stepping bend is probably a primary crustal feature. While the paleomagnetic data from each locality are well grouped close to a time- averaged axial dipole field direction, several aspects of the data and the units sampled suggest that the characteristic magnetizations indeed reflect intrusive events in this area in Late Cretaceous time. The data may be used to infer amounts of Late Cretaceous and younger de- formation in the area. First, each pluton and the associated magnetic mineralogy is at most only slightly altered. The only change in the primary, magmatic magnetic mineralogy of each pluton is a very weak martitization (hematite replacement of magnetite). Second, we have recorded mag- netization components of both normal and reverse polarity which we believe to be of TRM origin in the Water Canyon and Gillis Canyon plutons. The very recording of field reversals by these plutons unfortu- nately may have added to the overall dis- persion of the TRM components. The stratigraphic interval of the Columbia River basalt group that is the focus of this investigation consists of the lower flows of the Frenchmans Springs member [Mackin, 1961] of the Wanapum basalt formation (Figure 1). Geo- logic criteria including field relations, petrography, and chemistry show that the Frenchmans Springs member exists over a large portion of the Columbia River Plateau (Figure 2). This process of distributed shear is similar to that proposed by Beck [1980] to explain tectonic transport of displaced crustal fragments of the Cordillera. However, in this case, the zone of distributed shear is within the Ginkgo flows of the Wanapum Basalt member rather than between discontinuous crustal fragments. The hypothesis that there is distrib- uted shear throughout the Columbia Plateau, southwestern Washington, and the Oregon coast requires that the structural geology of this region be fairly complex. Structural elements that may have facili- tated this deformation are numerous and include (1) abundant north and northwest trending dextral strike slip faults of the Columbia Plateau and adjacent Cascade Range [Bentley and Anderson, 1979] and (2) east to northeast trending folds in the same area [Bentley, 1977, 1980; Campbell and Bentley, 1981]. Movement on these structures has been continuous since 16 m.y.B.P. with major pulses at 14-13 m.y.B.P. and 9-7 m.y.B.P. [Bentley et al., 1980]. The same workers have suggested that a similar structural style existed as early as Late Eocene time. Therefore the tectonic mecha

he Ginkgo flows, with their anomalous paleomagnetic direction and large areal distribution, provide the necessary paleomagnetic data to support the hypothesis that distributed shear has also contributed to tectonic rotations of the Pacific Northwest. In summary, paleomagnetic data from the Ginkgo flows of the Columbia River basalt Group suggest the prevailing tec- tonic mechanism for Columbia River Plateau and Oregon and Washington coast deformation, at least since 14 m.y.B.P., may well be southwestward increasing clockwise rotation about a nearby verti- cal axis, not a simple rotation of one large tectonic block. The driving force for this deformation is coupling between the North American and Farallon plates. Acknowledgments. Many thanks are due to (1) R. D. The direction of remanent magnetization for 102 sites in Eocene volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks of the O'Brien Creek Formation, Sanpoll Volcanics, and Klondike Mountain Formation suggests approximately 25 ø of clockwise rotation of a 100 by 200 km area in northeastern Washington. The volcanic rocks consist chiefly of rhyodacite and quartz latite flows, with intercalated ash flow tuff and volcaniclastic layers. These rocks have been sampled at 102 sites distributed among five volcanotectonic depressions: the Toroda Creek, Republic, Keller, and First Thought grabens and the Spokane-Enterprise lineament. The volcanic rocks probably range in age from 55 m.y. to about 48 m.y., and the 50- to 48-m.y.-old volcanic rocks within this suite appear to be rotated as much as the older rocks. Previous investigators have shown that 40-m.y.-old and younger plutonic rocks of northwestern Washington are not rotated; hence we infer that the north-central Washington rocks were rotated to their present declination between 48 and 40 m.y.B.P. (during the middle and/or late Eocene).

Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: TECTONICS, VOL. 4, NO. 6, PAGES 565-585, OCTOBER 1985 PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS FROM HONDURAS AND THEIR BEARING ON CARIBBEAN TECTONICS Wulf A. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. GENERAL GEOLOGY AND PROCEDURES The exposed rocks in Honduras define three major sequences: a poorly mapped metamorphic basement of Paleozoic or older age, a Mesozoic (mainly Cretaceous) sedi- mentary suite of clastic and carbonaceous rocks, and a volcanic sequence, dominated by ignimbrites, of Tertiary age [Elvir, 1974]. The Mesozoic stratigraphy of cen- tral Honduras, the only part of the Repub- lic that has been mapped to any detail, has been described by Finch [1981]. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. GEOLOGICAL SETTING The Late Precambrian and Early Paleozoic geological sequence preserved in Cape Breton Island, summarized in Figures 1 and 2, comprises Late Hadrynian basement volcanics and granites overlain by well- preserved Cambrian to Lower Ordovician shallow-water marine clastics and volcanics. The lithologic and faunal characteristics of these rocks and their correlation with similar strata found along strike in the northern Appalachians, particularly in eastern Newfoundland (see Figure la), have been discussed by many authors [e.g., Henningsmoen, 1969; Rast et al., 1976; Williams, 1978]. The assemblage of often geographically separate localities where similar rocks occur has been called the Avalon terrane by Williams and Hatcher [1983], named after the Avalon peninsula of Newfoundland. The Cambrian volcanics present in the Boisdale Peninsula (Bourinot Group) were the principal focus of our study. These volcanics comprise flows and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks, which appear to have had a restricted areal extent at the time they were formed [Keppie and Dostal, 1980; Hutchinson, 1952]. GEOLOGICAL SETTING The Late Precambrian and Early Paleozoic geological sequence preserved in Cape Breton Island, summarized in Figures 1 and 2, comprises Late Hadrynian basement volcanics and granites overlain by well- preserved Cambrian to Lower Ordovician shallow-water marine clastics and volcanics. The lithologic and faunal characteristics of these rocks and their correlation with similar strata found along strike in the northern Appalachians, particularly in eastern Newfoundland (see Figure la), have been discussed by many authors [e.g., Henningsmoen, 1969; Rast et al., 1976; Williams, 1978]. The assemblage of often geographically separate localities where similar rocks occur has been called the Avalon terrane by Williams and Hatcher [1983], named after the Avalon peninsula of Newfoundland. The Cambrian volcanics present in the Boisdale Peninsula (Bourinot Group) were the principal focus of our study. These volcanics comprise flows and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks, which appear to have had a restricted areal extent at the time they were formed [Keppie and Dostal, 1980; Hutchinson, 1952]. GEOLOGICAL SETTING The Late Precambrian and Early Paleozoic geological sequence preserved in Cape Breton Island, summarized in Figures 1 and 2, comprises Late Hadrynian basement volcanics and granites overlain by well- preserved Cambrian to Lower Ordovician shallow-water marine clastics and volcanics. The lithologic and faunal characteristics of these rocks and their correlation with similar strata found along strike in the northern Appalachians, particularly in eastern Newfoundland (see Figure la), have been discussed by many authors [e.g., Henningsmoen, 1969; Rast et al., 1976; Williams, 1978]. The assemblage of often geographically separate localities where similar rocks occur has been called the Avalon terrane by Williams and Hatcher [1983], named after the Avalon peninsula of Newfoundland. The Cambrian volcanics present in the Boisdale Peninsula (Bourinot Group) were the principal focus of our study. These volcanics comprise flows and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks, which appear to have had a restricted areal extent at the time they were formed [Keppie and Dostal, 1980; Hutchinson, 1952]. They have been related 632 Johnson and Van der Voo: Cambrian Paleomagnetism, Avalon by Hutchinson [1952] to a volcanic

enschist facies. Initial reconnaissance sampling in the Bourinot Group was concentrated in sediments of varying lithology exposed in the stream sections along Gregwa, Dugald, Macmullin, and Gillis Brooks. Different lithologies represented here probably reflect varying source materials since fossils preserved in different beds are similar [Hutchinson, 1952]. These streams were later resampled in detail (see Figure 1) with each site restricted to a single bed or a few beds with similar lithology. Volcanic flows immediately underlying or interbedded with sediments were sampled at Dugald and Gillis Brooks (see Figures lc and ld), as well as in the north part of the study area. A similar agglomerate unit was sampled at Gregwa Brook (site B01) and at MacMullin Brook (B25) and may represent the same unit [Hutchinson, 1952]; however, other stratigraphic units, whether volcanic or sedimentary, were not uniquely correlated between localities. From the orthogonal plots and the PCA the multicomponent nature of the magnetizations present in these volcanics was apparent. Both magnetite and haematite are major remanence carriers. The selection criteria applied to the PCA directions was designed to eliminate spurious components as far as possible due to viscous remanent magnetization (VRM) or isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM). Additional paleomagnetic data from the north-central Rio Grande rift support previous suggestions for counterclockwise rotation of a large crustal block. Thirteen sites from intrusive and extrusive rocks associated with the Oligocene Espinaso Formation in the area around the Ortiz Mountains, central New Mexico, yield magnetic directions of I = 42.1ø and D = 337.80 (alpha-95 = 10.3ø). Comparison with the expected direction for the Oligocene indicates 17.80 + 11.40 of counterclockwise rotation. This agrees with previous studies of Miocene to Pliocene rocks north of the study area that also show about 150 of counterclockwise rotation and corroborates the timing of this motion as post 5 Ma. This agrees with previous studies of Miocene to Pliocene rocks north of the study area that also show about 150 of counterclockwise rotation and corroborates the timing of this motion as post 5 Ma. The extent of the rotated block now includes areas in and adjacent to the Espanola basin east of the Pajarito fault zone, from the San Luis basin in the north to the Albuquerque basin in the south. Extensive published geologic and structural information indicates that counterclockwise block rotation in the Rio Grande rift probably results from left slip along the rift. Structural consequences of the counterclockwise block rotation are uplift at the acute ends (Sandia and Picuris uplifts) and subsidence at the obtuse ends (Velarde graben and Santa Fe embayment ).

Specifically, rocks west of the Pajarito fault zone are rotated 15 o clockwise, whereas rocks east of the fault zone are rotated counterclockwise a similar amount. These results are based on paleomagnetic studies of four volcanic units in the Jemez Mountains (Paliza Canyon Formation, Lobato Basalt, Tschicoma Formation [Brown and Golombek, 1985] and Vailes Rhyolite Doell et al., 1968]) and three studies east of the fault (Chamita Formation [MacFadden, 1977], Tesuque Fromation [Barghoorn, 1981], and Cerros del Rio Volcanics Brown and Golombek, 1985]). Because the rotations of Miocene and older rocks are roughly the same, the initiation of rotation must have begun after the Miocene, about 5 Ma. Differential rotation across the fault zone is about 4 o per million years. GEOLOGIC SETTING œntrusive and extrusive igneous rocks of mid-Tertiary age crop out along the eastern edge of the Rio Grande rift between the Sandia Mountains to the south and the Sangre de Cristo Mountains to the north (Figure 1). These outcrops include intrusive rocks in the Ortiz Mountains and Cerrillos Hills and extrusive flows in the Hagan embayment, in the Cienega area, and in Arroyo Hondo south of Santa Fe. The intrusive rocks are found within a sequence of prerift Mesozoic and early Cenozoic sedimentary rocks. Extrusive rocks overlie the Eocene Galisteo Formation [Stearns, 1943], and in turn are overlain by rift sediments of the Santa Fe Group. Igneous activity appears to have occurred prior to rifting, although the youngest volcanics may be contemporaneous with the early stages of rifting. From successfully tested samples, two major remanence components, both of dual polarity, can be recognized (denoted groups A and B). Group A constitutes the principal and intermediate to high-blocking remanence in both pre-Devonian and Devonian rocks and is characterized by shallow to intermediate dipping magnetizations with NE-SW declinations (Figures 5 and 6). Precambrian and Lower Palaeozoic samples exhibit blocking temperatures and directio- nal stability up to 680øC, but a number of samples are characterized by distributed and almost total unblocking below 580øC and define essentially single component group A remanences (Figure 5b and 6b). Dual- polarity interplay (group A remanences) is notably, particularly in the Devonian samples, and may in addition be masked by group B remanences (see below), thus complicating the isolation of characteris- tic remanence components. The exposed sedimentary rocks of southern Umnak Island (Figure 2b) consist of about 300 m of thin-bedded laminated siltstone, mudstone, and very fine grained sandstone of mainly volcaniclastic composition. Strata are gently folded and dips rarely exceed 10 ø . The thickest, most continuous exposures are along Driftwood Bay and Starr Point where palynomorphs and dinofiagellates suggest a late Eocene to early Oligocene age of deposition [McLean and Hein, 1984]. Siltstone and mudstone consist of varying proportions of tuff (glassy volcanic debris) and angular grains of calcic plagioclase, rare quartz, augitc, and opaque minerals. In most rocks the tuffaceous component is altered to smectite and more rarely to zeolite minerals, while calcic plagioclase and augitc remain unaltered. A low-temperature diagenesis of the sediments is suggested by preservation of calcic plagioclase, the presence of low-temperature zeolites (heulandite and analcime), and light-colored palynomorphs. The exposed sedimentary rocks of southern Umnak Island (Figure 2b) consist of about 300 m of thin-bedded laminated siltstone, mudstone, and very fine grained sandstone of mainly volcaniclastic composition. Strata are gently folded and dips rarely exceed 10 ø . The thickest, most continuous exposures are along Driftwood Bay and Starr Point where palynomorphs and dinofiagellates suggest a late Eocene to early Oligocene age of deposition [McLean and Hein, 1984]. Siltstone and mudstone consist of varying proportions of tuff (glassy volcanic debris) and angular grains of calcic plagioclase, rare quartz, augitc, and opaque minerals. In most rocks the tuffaceous component is altered to smectite and more rarely to zeolite minerals, while calcic plagioclase and augitc remain unaltered. A low-temperature diagenesis of the sediments is suggested by preservation of calcic plagioclase, the presence of low-temperature zeolites (heulandite and analcime), and light-colored palynomorphs. A quartz diorite stock is present along the south shore of Driftwood Bay at Cape Udak, (U/Pb age, 30.4 q- 1.5 Ma), and 13 m.y. old dikes of dark gray pyroxene basaltic andesitc and pyroxene andesitc cut the sedimentary rocks of Driftwood Bay and Starr Point [McLean and Hein, 1984]. Sedimentary rocks of late Eocene to early Oligocene age from the Aleutian Islands, have been paleomagnetically studied to determine the paleolatitude of this island arc. Samples were collected from gently dipping, thin-bedded, laminated siltstone, mudstone, and very fine grained sandstone of marine origin. After demagnetization, samples from each locality showed both polarities of a remanent magnetization that thermal, isothermal remanent magnetization, and Js-T experiments suggest is carried by magnetite. After tectonic correction, the cos decreases in both localities, suggesting magnetization was acquired before folding of the beds. The characteristic magnetization shows that no significant poleward motion of the Aleutian arc has occurred with respect to the North American plate since the early Oligocene (Amlia, F---4 ø , AF:5 ø; Umnak, F----0.8 o, AF:3.5 o ), but the declinations are rotated significantly clockwise (Amlia, R=70 ø , AR--23 o; Umnak, R----36.

The characteristic magnetization shows that no significant poleward motion of the Aleutian arc has occurred with respect to the North American plate since the early Oligocene (Amlia, F---4 ø , AF:5 ø; Umnak, F----0.8 o, AF:3.5 o ), but the declinations are rotated significantly clockwise (Amlia, R=70 ø , AR--23 o; Umnak, R----36.7 ø, AR--11.2 ø ). Using these paleomagnetic data, relevant Euler poles, and hotspot locations, we propose a new model for the formation of the Zodiac fan. In this model, the start of Zodiac fan deposition corresponds to accretionary, igneous, and erosional events in the Pacific Northwest and fragmentation of the Farallon plate along the margin of the North American plate into small plates. Recent paleomagnetic studies of samples from the Aleutian arc have suggested poleward translation of between 0 and 1440 km (Figure 1, Table 1) since the middle Tertiary [Stone, 1972, 1975; Hillhouse and Gromme, 1977; Panuska, 1980; Stone et al., 1982a, b; Harbert et al., 1984]. This early paleomagnetic data from the Peninsular and Prince William terranes in southern Alaska (Figure 1) suggested that these terranes may not have accreted to the North American plate until the middle or late Tertiary [Stone and Packer, 1977, 1979; Stone et al., 1982a]. However, thermal alteration of sampled units, complex geological structure, and demagnetization of only a small number of samples made tectonic interpretation of many of the previous paleomagnetic studies difficult [Coe et al., 1985]. In addition, the geometry of the large Zodiac sediment fan in the northeast Pacific basin suggests poleward transport of the Aleutian arc [Scholl et al., 1977; Byrne, 1979; Stevenson et al., 1983; Moore et al., 1983]. In this paper we do not attempt to formulate a new tectonic model; rather, the objective of our study is to provide a new and independent paleomagnetic data set by which various aspects of proposed models may be tested. SAMPLING LOCALITIES We have collected samples from three widely separated localities in Haiti. These are designated from north to south as Ennery, Beloc, and Les Cayes [Figure 1]. A \"locality\" consists of several sites, each of which in turn represents 7-11 cored samples. Sites within a locality are distributed about an area of a few square kilometers; a distri- bution that will become important in our final synthesis and interpretation of the paleomagnetic data. Samples were obtained in the field using a portable rock coring drill. At the Beloc locality we used the oriented-block method to collect the less consolidated chalk lithologies. All orientations were made using the Brunton compass, and at each site we were careful to sample only the freshest appearing materials. An almost complete sequence of strata with ages from early Paleogene to Quaternary is well preserved in the Oga Peninsula, on the western side of northeast Honshu at about t0 ø north latitude (Figure 1), making the Oga Peninsula a type locality for the Ter- tiary sequence in Northeast Japan. Tertiary formations, arranged in monoclinal beds of strata, are well exposed along the west coast of the penin- sula (Figure lb). Geological units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. cal units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. The most recent vokanic rocks are Kanpuzan lava flows erupted in the Quaternary. As shown in Figure 2, over 30 age determinations made by different methods (K-At and fission track methods) give consistent results [Kaneoka, 1983a]. We adopted as the age of each formation the mean value of the reported ages as suggested by Kaneoka [1983a]. The ages of the younger sedimentary formations were estimated from biostratigraphic studies as sumrealized by Tsuchl [1981]. Previous paleomagnetic studies in the Oga Peninsula were mainly concerned with the magnetostratigraphy of the younger sedimentary rocks [Kent, 1973; Kimura, 1974; Kitazato, 1975]. In this area, a total of 26 sites were sampled, and six or more core samples were obtained at each site by using a gasoline-powered drilling apparatus. An almost complete sequence of strata with ages from early Paleogene to Quaternary is well preserved in the Oga Peninsula, on the western side of northeast Honshu at about t0 ø north latitude (Figure 1), making the Oga Peninsula a type locality for the Ter- tiary sequence in Northeast Japan. Tertiary formations, arranged in monoclinal beds of strata, are well exposed along the west coast of the penin- sula (Figure lb). Geological units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. cal units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. The most recent vokanic rocks are Kanpuzan lava flows erupted in the Quaternary. As shown in Figure 2, over 30 age determinations made by different methods (K-At and fission track methods) give consistent results [Kaneoka, 1983a]. We adopted as the age of each formation the mean value of the reported ages as suggested by Kaneoka [1983a]. The ages of the younger sedimentary formations were estimated from biostratigraphic studies as sumrealized by Tsuchl [1981]. Previous paleomagnetic studies in the Oga Peninsula were mainly concerned with the magnetostratigraphy of the younger sedimentary rocks [Kent, 1973; Kimura, 1974; Kitazato, 1975]. In this area, a total of 26 sites were sampled, and six or more core samples were obtained at each site by using a gasoline-powered drilling apparatus. cal units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: The vokanic sequences in the peninsula are interstratified with thin sed- imentary layers. The paleohorizontal plane of these rocks was estimated from the interbedded sedimentary rocks near the sampling sites. Foliations of the included pumice or ash (entaxitic texture; [Ross and Smith, 1961]) are dis- cernible in welded tuffs and were also used for estimating the paleohorizonal plane. EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES Specimens which are 2.5 cm in diameter and about 2.3 cm in length were cut from the collected core samples. The remanence was measured using a Schonstedt SSM-1A spin- ner magnetometer. Because of the weak intensities of the magnetization, telLfold to twentyfold stacking of the output signal was required for the sedimentary rocks. Progressive AF and thermal demagnetizations were carried out to ob- tain stable components. Heating for the thermal demag- netization was performed in a slow flow of nitrogen gas in order to prevent chemical changes of the ferromagnetic minerals in the samples. The results of the progressive demagnetization were plotted on orthogonal vector dia- grams [Zijderveld, 1967], and stable and soft components of magnetization were calculated from the least squares fit of straight lines. An almost complete sequence of strata with ages from early Paleogene to Quaternary is well preserved in the Oga Peninsula, on the western side of northeast Honshu at about t0 ø north latitude (Figure 1), making the Oga Peninsula a type locality for the Ter- tiary sequence in Northeast Japan. Tertiary formations, arranged in monoclinal beds of strata, are well exposed along the west coast of the penin- sula (Figure lb). Geological units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. cal units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. The most recent vokanic rocks are Kanpuzan lava flows erupted in the Quaternary. As shown in Figure 2, over 30 age determinations made by different methods (K-At and fission track methods) give consistent results [Kaneoka, 1983a]. We adopted as the age of each formation the mean value of the reported ages as suggested by Kaneoka [1983a]. The ages of the younger sedimentary formations were estimated from biostratigraphic studies as sumrealized by Tsuchl [1981]. Previous paleomagnetic studies in the Oga Peninsula were mainly concerned with the magnetostratigraphy of the younger sedimentary rocks [Kent, 1973; Kimura, 1974; Kitazato, 1975]. In this area, a total of 26 sites were sampled, and six or more core samples were obtained at each site by using a gasoline-powered drilling apparatus.
